en.title: Entrepreneurship: the whole course
en.short: What an entrepreneurship degree, HND or module covers, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Entrepreneurship is the process of spotting an opportunity, gathering resources and taking on risk to create something of value. The value may be commercial, social or both. The subject studies how people and organisations do this: how they find and test ideas, build a business model, raise money, sell, operate and grow. It also studies why ventures fail, and what can be learned from failure.

It is not only about starting a company. Intrapreneurs do similar work inside an established organisation. Social entrepreneurs pursue a mission and earn income. Family businesses face their own questions of governance and succession.

Entrepreneurship draws on economics, psychology, finance, marketing, law and strategy. It is taught through theory, cases and, above all, practice. You will be asked to do the numbers, not only describe the idea.

sections.heading: How study is usually organised
sections.text:
Awards and lengths differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. Common awards are a BSc or BA in Entrepreneurship or Business Administration, an HND or ND at polytechnics, and at postgraduate level an MSc, an MBA or a PhD.

In Nigeria, universities and polytechnics follow national benchmarks, and many institutions require a general entrepreneurship course for all students, whatever their main subject. Degree students also take modules in accounting, economics, marketing and law. In the United Kingdom and South Africa, entrepreneurship is often a module inside a business or commerce degree, and some institutions offer it as a named degree.

Most programmes mix lectures with case discussions, guest speakers, group projects and a business plan or venture project. Postgraduate study adds theory and research methods, and usually a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The course opens with the basics: what entrepreneurship is, the entrepreneurial mindset, creativity and idea generation, opportunity recognition and screening, market research and customer discovery, business model design, business calculations, legal forms and registration, and writing a business plan and pitch.

The core stage tests whether an idea can work. Feasibility analysis leads to a go or no-go decision. Then come marketing for new ventures, sales and customer development, operations and supply, financial management, sources of finance, venture capital and valuation, and managing a small business. Later topics cover growth and scaling, digital entrepreneurship and e-commerce, social entrepreneurship, family business, intrapreneurship, ethics and social responsibility, risk and failure, and exit strategies.

At master’s level the focus shifts to theory, research methods, entrepreneurial ecosystems and policy, and technology entrepreneurship and innovation systems.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study entrepreneurship by doing. Turn each topic into a small task: interview five potential customers, sketch a business model canvas, price a product, build a cash flow forecast. Keep the arithmetic honest and show your assumptions.

Read cases with a question in mind: what decision did the founder face, and what would you have done? Compare the case with a local business you know. Notice what the textbook says and what the evidence shows.

Use current local sources for company law, tax and registration, because these differ by country. For academic topics, read the original articles rather than summaries.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
The most common mistake is treating an idea as an opportunity without testing it. Students also skip customer conversations, overestimate sales, and ignore cash flow and unit economics. A venture can be profitable on paper and still run out of cash.

Other errors include:
Confusing a business plan with a pitch deck.
Assuming funding is the main problem when the offer is weak.
Treating one country’s company law or tax rule as universal.
Copying a foreign case without checking whether the market is the same.
Ignoring the team, and the ethics of the venture.

keyPoints: Entrepreneurship is the process of finding an opportunity, gathering resources and taking risk to create value.
An idea becomes an opportunity only when customers show they will pay.
The course moves from mindset and ideas, through feasibility and finance, to growth and exit.
Do the numbers: price, costs, cash flow and unit economics decide whether a venture survives.
Company law, tax and registration rules belong to one country, so check local sources.
Funding rarely fixes a weak offer; customers do.

en.title: Introduction: Entrepreneurship and the Entrepreneur
en.short: Definitions, enterprise versus entrepreneurship, types, economic role, myths and the idea-to-venture process.

sections.heading: Definitions
sections.text: Entrepreneurship is the process of spotting an opportunity, gathering and organising resources, and creating value while accepting uncertainty and risk. An entrepreneur is the person who does this: decides, coordinates people and money, and bears the possible loss. The word is wider than starting a business. It can occur inside an existing organisation, called intrapreneurship.

sections.heading: Enterprise and types
sections.text: Enterprise can mean a business organisation, or a bold undertaking. Entrepreneurship is the activity or process; an enterprise is often the vehicle or result. Types include opportunity entrepreneurship, where the founder chooses a venture, and necessity entrepreneurship, where a lack of other income pushes the founder. Other useful types are small business, scalable start-up, which aims for rapid growth, and social enterprise, which pursues a social mission alongside income.

sections.heading: Economic role and myths
sections.text: New ventures can create jobs, introduce products and methods, increase competition and support supply chains. They also fail often, so their net effect varies. A venture may also improve local skills and tax revenue, but evidence differs by context. Myths to correct: entrepreneurs are not only born, not only gamblers, not only young tech founders, and not only rich people. Most learn by doing, manage risk rather than seek it, and many run ordinary local firms.

sections.heading: From idea to venture
sections.text: The process usually runs from idea generation, through opportunity screening and customer research, to a business model, a plan, funding, launch, and learning from feedback. The process is not linear; founders often return to earlier steps. A simple case: Chidi in Enugu notices offices lack reliable lunch delivery. He tests the idea with ten offices, finds demand, starts with one kitchen and two riders, and adjusts prices after feedback. He has moved from an idea to a small venture.

keyPoints: Entrepreneurship is the process of pursuing an opportunity and creating value under risk.
An entrepreneur identifies the opportunity, organises resources and bears possible loss.
Enterprise is often the business or undertaking; entrepreneurship is the activity.
Types include opportunity, necessity, small business, scalable start-up and social enterprise.
New ventures can create jobs and innovation, but many fail, so effects vary.
The process runs from idea to screening, model, plan, funding, launch and learning, and is not linear.

en.title: The entrepreneurial mindset
en.short: Motivation, opportunity alertness, self-efficacy, risk propensity, achievement, resilience and learning from setbacks.

sections.heading: What mindset means
sections.text: The entrepreneurial mindset is a set of attitudes and habits that lead a person to notice opportunities, act on them and keep adjusting. Some parts are relatively stable traits, such as a general tendency to seek achievement. Others are learned skills, such as asking customers good questions or keeping records. No single personality type is required. Studies find entrepreneurs differ widely, and many successful owners are cautious, sociable or quiet in different ways.

sections.heading: Motivation and alertness
sections.text: Motivation is the reason a person starts and continues. It may be pull motivation, such as wanting independence or solving a problem, or push motivation, such as unemployment or low pay. Need for achievement is the desire to meet a standard of excellence; it can support enterprise, but it is not essential and can become perfectionism. Opportunity alertness is the habit of noticing unmet needs, waste or inefficiency. It improves with experience, networks and deliberate practice, not only with natural talent.

sections.heading: Confidence and risk
sections.text: Self-efficacy is a person’s belief that they can carry out a specific task. It is not general bravado; it grows from practice, role models and small wins. Risk propensity is the willingness to accept uncertain outcomes. Entrepreneurs are not all high risk takers. Research is mixed, and sensible founders often reduce risk by testing cheaply. In a case, Ngozi in Enugu, Nigeria, sees offices skipping lunch. She tests 20 packed lunches for one office, asks for feedback and changes the menu before buying more equipment.

sections.heading: Resilience and learning
sections.text: Resilience is the ability to cope, adapt and continue after setbacks. It does not mean ignoring loss. Learning from setbacks means reviewing what happened, separating bad luck from bad decisions, and changing the next action. Ngozi’s first week brings 12 orders, not 20. She records why customers refused, finds that delivery was late, and arranges earlier cooking. That is a learning cycle, not proof of a special personality.

keyPoints: The entrepreneurial mindset mixes traits with learned skills, and no single personality type is essential.
Motivation may be pull, such as independence, or push, such as unemployment.
Need for achievement is the desire to meet a standard of excellence, but it is not essential.
Opportunity alertness is noticing unmet needs and inefficiencies, and it improves with practice.
Self-efficacy is task-specific confidence; risk propensity is willingness to accept uncertainty, and it varies.
Resilience and learning from setbacks mean reviewing what happened and changing the next action.

en.title: Creativity, Innovation and Idea Generation
en.short: Creativity techniques, four innovation types, and how ideas are screened before they become opportunities.

sections.heading: Creativity and innovation
sections.text: Creativity is the ability to produce original and useful ideas. Innovation is turning a useful idea into something delivered and adopted, such as a product, service or method. Creativity supplies the raw idea; innovation adds testing, resources and execution. An idea is not yet an opportunity. An opportunity is an idea that meets a real customer need and can be pursued with available resources.

sections.heading: Practical techniques
sections.text: Brainstorming gathers a group to produce many ideas without judging them at first. Criticism is delayed; quantity is encouraged; wild ideas are welcome; ideas are combined and improved. Mind mapping starts with a central word and branches into related words, making links visible. Observation means watching people use products or do tasks, then noting delays, workarounds and complaints. A small example: Ngozi, a campus food seller, watches students queue at lunch. She maps branches such as speed, price, payment and location, then brainstorms prepaid orders and a second serving point.

sections.heading: Types of innovation
sections.text: Product innovation changes what is offered, such as a new drink or app. Process innovation changes how work is done, such as mobile ordering that cuts queues. Organisational innovation changes structure or routines, such as giving staff weekly improvement meetings. Business model innovation changes how value is created, delivered and captured, such as charging a subscription instead of a one-off fee. These types can combine.

sections.heading: Screening ideas
sections.text: Screening is a quick filter before spending much money. Ask: does it solve a real problem for a defined customer? Can we make and deliver it? Can it cover costs and earn a margin? What evidence would change our mind? Ngozi screens prepaid orders: students want speed, she can run it by phone, and the fee covers costs. She tests it for two weeks before buying equipment. This separates a creative idea from a tested opportunity.

keyPoints: Creativity produces original and useful ideas; innovation turns such ideas into adopted products, processes or models.
Brainstorming separates idea generation from judgement, while mind mapping makes connections visible.
Observation of real users reveals delays, workarounds and unmet needs.
Product, process, organisational and business model innovation change different parts of a venture.
An idea becomes an opportunity only when it meets a real customer need and can be pursued with available resources.
Screen ideas quickly for customer need, feasibility and viability before investing money.

en.title: Opportunity Recognition and Screening
en.short: How to tell an idea from an opportunity, find sources and screen for need, timing, competition and fit.

sections.heading: Idea or opportunity
sections.text: An idea is a thought about a product, service or method. An opportunity is an idea that is attractive, timely and durable enough to create value for paying customers. The difference is evidence. A clever idea may lack a market, a route to customers or a team able to deliver. Not every idea is an opportunity.

sections.heading: Where opportunities come from
sections.text: Opportunities often appear where there is a problem, a change or a gap. Problems include delays, high costs and poor service. Changes in technology, regulation, population, income or taste can create new needs. Gaps appear when existing firms are slow, expensive or absent in an area. A growing estate with no reliable delivery service is one local example. What matters is evidence that people will pay.

sections.heading: Screening criteria
sections.text: Screening tests whether an idea deserves time and money. Market need asks whether customers have a real problem and will pay. Timing asks whether the window of opportunity is open. That window is the period when conditions allow entry before competitors arrive or the need fades. Competition asks what customers use now and how hard entry is. Fit asks whether founders have the skills, contacts, resources and values to execute. A good idea can fail if demand is too small, timing is wrong, rivals are strong or the team cannot deliver at a cost customers accept.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Consider Amina, a student in Kano. Classmates queue for printing before deadlines. Her idea is a campus printing and binding service. Need seems real, but she must check how many students pay, what they pay and whether demand lasts all term. Timing may be good if the campus is expanding. Competition includes two nearby shops and a departmental printer. Fit is fair because she designs documents, but she lacks space and capital. If rent and machine costs leave no margin at the price students accept, the idea is not viable. Screening sends her back to test demand and costs before committing.

keyPoints: An idea becomes an opportunity only when evidence shows paying customers, a route to them and a team able to deliver.
Opportunities often come from problems, changes and gaps left by existing firms.
The window of opportunity is the period when conditions allow entry before rivals arrive or need fades.
Screen opportunities for market need, timing, competition and founder fit.
A good idea is not viable if demand is too small, margins too thin or the team cannot execute.
Screening reduces risk but does not replace testing with real customers.

en.title: Market research and customer discovery
en.short: How to test customer assumptions with interviews, surveys, observation, secondary data and simple sampling.

sections.heading: Testing assumptions
sections.text:
Market research is the organised collection of information about customers, competitors and markets. Customer discovery is a narrow, early form: talking to potential customers to test your assumptions before you build.

Write down what you believe. Who is the customer? What problem do they have? How often? What do they use now? What is their willingness to pay, the most they would pay? Each belief is an assumption, something you accept without proof. Discovery tries to prove or disprove it with evidence, not opinion.

sections.heading: Four methods
sections.text:
Four methods are common. A customer interview is a short conversation with open questions about past behaviour, not a sales pitch. A survey asks the same questions to many people, online or on paper; keep it short and avoid leading questions.

Observation means watching what people do, like which stall they visit or what they carry. Secondary data is information already collected by others, such as national statistics, trade reports or competitor prices. It is cheap but may be out of date or about a different group.

sections.heading: Sampling and bias
sections.text:
Sampling means studying a small group to learn about a larger population. A random sample gives every member an equal chance of selection, so it is more representative. A convenience sample uses whoever is easy to reach, such as your classmates, and can be biased. Bias means a result that is systematically wrong.

Friends and family are convenient but often polite and unrepresentative; they may praise your idea and still not buy. Use them for practice, not proof.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text:
A made-up case: Amina plans to sell phone chargers near a college in Ibadan. She assumes students will pay ₦2,000. She interviews 15 students, surveys 60 at random from a list of 600, and observes two phone shops.

She finds many students pay about ₦1,500 and buy from a market stall. Her assumption was wrong. She changes her price and supplier before spending money. The survey sample was 60 ÷ 600 = 10% of the list.

keyPoints: Customer discovery tests your assumptions about customers before you invest.
Use interviews, surveys, observation and secondary data together, not one method alone.
A random sample is more representative than a convenience sample.
Friends and family are biased and should not be your only evidence.
Willingness to pay is best estimated from past purchases and current spending, not from polite opinions.
Secondary data is cheap but may be out of date or about another group.

en.title: Business Models and the Business Model Canvas
en.short: How to describe a venture with the Business Model Canvas and Lean Canvas, and test key assumptions.

sections.heading: Model on one page
sections.text: A business model explains how a venture creates value for customers and captures some of that value as income. It is not a dated plan; it is a summary of choices. The Business Model Canvas, by Alexander Osterwalder and Yves Pigneur, puts nine blocks on one page: customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships and cost structure. Customer segments are groups with shared needs. The value proposition is why they buy. Channels are how you reach and sell. Customer relationships are how you keep them. Revenue streams are how money comes in. Cost structure is the main costs. Key resources are assets and people; key activities are critical tasks.

sections.heading: Lean Canvas
sections.text: The Lean Canvas, by Ash Maurya, adapts the canvas for new ventures. It replaces key partners, key activities, key resources and customer relationships with problem, solution, key metrics and unfair advantage. It also uses a unique value proposition. This focuses attention on risk: which problem, for whom, and what measurable sign shows progress. Key metrics are the few numbers that show whether the model works.

sections.heading: Riskiest assumptions
sections.text: A canvas is a set of guesses. List assumptions, rank them by importance and evidence, and test the riskiest first. Use cheap experiments: customer interviews, a landing page, a prototype or a pre-sale. Define pass or fail before the test. Example: a student meal service in Lagos charges ₦2,500 a meal. Food and delivery cost ₦1,500 a meal, so the contribution per meal (price minus variable cost) is ₦1,000. Fixed costs are ₦300,000 a month. Break-even = 300,000 ÷ 1,000 = 300 meals a month. Test: can you sell 300 meals a month? At 500 meals, profit = 500 × 1,000 − 300,000 = ₦200,000. If the test fails, change the segment, price or channel, then update the canvas.

keyPoints: A business model explains how a venture creates, delivers and captures value.
The Business Model Canvas has nine blocks, including customer segments, value proposition, channels, revenue streams and cost structure.
The Lean Canvas replaces some BMC blocks with problem, solution, key metrics and unfair advantage for early-stage testing.
A canvas is a set of assumptions, not proof.
Test the riskiest assumptions first with cheap experiments and clear pass or fail rules.
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit; profit = units × contribution − fixed costs.

en.title: Business Calculations for Entrepreneurs
en.short: This summary covers revenue, cost, profit, margin, mark-up, break-even and simple cash-flow projections.

sections.heading: Revenue and cost
sections.text:
Revenue is money from sales before deductions: price × quantity sold. Costs are fixed (rent, salaries) or variable (materials, packaging). Total cost = fixed costs + variable cost per unit × quantity.

Example: a trader sells 30 bags at ₦10,000 each. Revenue = 30 × 10,000 = ₦300,000. Variable cost is ₦6,000 a bag and fixed costs are ₦80,000. Total cost = 80,000 + 30 × 6,000 = ₦260,000. Profit = 300,000 − 260,000 = ₦40,000.

sections.heading: Profit, margin, mark-up
sections.text:
Profit = revenue − total cost. Margin = profit ÷ revenue × 100, so it is profit as a share of selling price. Mark-up = profit ÷ cost × 100, so it is profit as a share of cost.

Using the same example: margin = 40,000 ÷ 300,000 × 100 = 13.3%. Mark-up = 40,000 ÷ 260,000 × 100 = 15.4%. A 15.4% mark-up gives a 13.3% margin, not the same figure.

sections.heading: Break-even point
sections.text:
Break-even point is the quantity where revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero. Contribution per unit = price − variable cost per unit. Break-even quantity = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit.

Example: price ₦10,000, variable cost ₦6,000, so contribution = ₦4,000. Fixed costs are ₦80,000. Break-even = 80,000 ÷ 4,000 = 20 bags. Check: revenue = 20 × 10,000 = ₦200,000; total cost = 80,000 + 20 × 6,000 = ₦200,000.

sections.heading: Cash flow vs profit
sections.text:
Cash flow is money actually received and paid. Profit is revenue minus costs, including credit sales and non-cash items such as depreciation (the fall in value of equipment over time). A credit sale can raise profit before any cash arrives, so profit and cash flow differ in timing.

A cash-flow projection lists expected receipts and payments by month. Closing cash = opening cash + receipts − payments. Example: opening ₦50,000, receipts ₦120,000, payments ₦140,000. Closing cash = 50,000 + 120,000 − 140,000 = ₦30,000. A negative closing balance signals a shortfall, even if the business is profitable.

keyPoints: Revenue = price × quantity sold; profit = revenue − total cost.
Margin = profit ÷ revenue × 100; mark-up = profit ÷ cost × 100.
Break-even quantity = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit).
Closing cash = opening cash + receipts − payments.
Profit includes credit sales and non-cash costs, but cash flow records actual money timing.
A profitable business can still run out of cash.

en.title: Legal forms, registration and compliance
en.short: Sole proprietorship, partnership, limited company and cooperative, plus registration, licences and tax.

sections.heading: Common legal forms
sections.text: A sole proprietorship is owned by one person. It is simple and cheap, but the owner has unlimited liability: personal assets can pay business debts. A partnership is owned by two or more partners who share profits and control. In a general partnership, partners usually have unlimited liability. A limited company is a separate legal person from its owners. Its shareholders have limited liability, usually limited to unpaid amounts on their shares. A cooperative is owned and controlled by its members, often with one member one vote, and it distributes surplus according to its rules. Limited liability means owners risk only what they agreed to invest, though fraud or breaking company law can remove protection.

sections.heading: Registration and licences
sections.text: Registration creates the legal record. In Nigeria, the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) registers business names and companies under the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020. In Ghana, the Office of the Registrar of Companies registers companies under the Companies Act 2019 (Act 992). Registration usually involves a name search, application, constitution or particulars, and a fee. Some activities need extra licences, such as food, health, transport or financial services, and local government permits. Cooperatives are registered under cooperative law with a designated registrar. Forms, fees and offices differ by country and change, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Tax and compliance
sections.text: After registration, the venture must register for tax, keep records, file returns and pay tax. In Nigeria, companies pay company income tax to the Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS), renamed the Nigeria Revenue Service from 2026, while sole traders pay personal income tax through the state internal revenue service. VAT rules apply. In Ghana, the Ghana Revenue Authority handles tax. Case: Amina trades as a sole proprietor in Kano. She registers a business name with CAC, obtains any local permit, keeps sales records and files personal income tax. If she later forms a private limited company, the company becomes the taxpayer and must file company returns, but her personal liability is limited. Compliance costs rise with formality.

keyPoints: A sole proprietorship has one owner and unlimited personal liability.
A limited company is a separate legal person, so shareholders normally have limited liability.
A cooperative is owned and controlled by its members, often one member one vote.
Registration and licences differ by country; in Nigeria the CAC registers companies and business names.
Tax duties differ by country; in Nigeria companies pay company income tax to FIRS (Nigeria Revenue Service from 2026) while sole traders pay personal income tax to the state.
Fees, forms and rules change, so check the current official source before registering.

en.title: Writing the Business Plan and Pitch
en.short: How to write a business plan, set milestones, project finances, assess risk and pitch to investors.

sections.heading: Purpose and audience
sections.text:
A business plan is a written description of a venture and how it will work. It tests and communicates the idea; it does not guarantee success.

An internal plan is a working document for founders and staff. It is candid about weaknesses and updated as evidence changes. An external plan goes to banks, investors or grant panels. It is formal, selective and backed by evidence, because readers compare proposals. The audience decides the detail: a bank wants repayment evidence; an equity investor wants growth and an exit.

Feasibility findings feed the plan by turning plausible assumptions into actions and numbers.

sections.heading: Sections and milestones
sections.text:
Most plans contain an executive summary, the problem and solution, market and customer evidence, the business model, operations, the team, milestones, financial projections, risk analysis and the funding request. The executive summary is written last and must stand alone.

A milestone is a dated, measurable target, such as 'register the business by month two' or 'reach 200 repeat customers by month six'. Financial projections include a cash flow forecast, profit projection and break-even estimate. Risk analysis names the main risks and gives a mitigation for each.

sections.heading: Projections, risk and pitch
sections.text:
Case: Amina plans a packaged spice business in Kano. Feasibility gives start-up costs of ₦1,200,000, monthly sales of ₦600,000, variable costs at 60% of sales and fixed costs of ₦150,000. Monthly contribution = 600,000 − 360,000 = ₦240,000. Monthly profit = 240,000 − 150,000 = ₦90,000. Break-even sales = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin ratio (the share of sales left after variable costs) = 150,000 ÷ 0.40 = ₦375,000 per month. Payback = 1,200,000 ÷ 90,000 = 13.3 months. Her plan lists risks such as spice price rises and late payments, each with a response.

A short investor pitch is a spoken summary; check the organiser’s time limit. It covers problem, solution, market evidence, business model, traction (customer take-up), team, and the amount requested with its use. The pitch opens a conversation; the plan supports due diligence, the funder’s detailed check of the business. End with one ask.

keyPoints: A business plan tests and communicates a venture; it is not a guarantee.
An internal plan is candid and updated; an external plan is formal and evidence-based for funders.
Main sections include the executive summary, market evidence, model, operations, team, milestones, projections, risks and funding request.
A milestone is a dated, measurable target.
Break-even sales = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin ratio; payback = start-up cost ÷ monthly profit.
A short pitch covers problem, solution, evidence, model, traction, team and the ask; the plan supports due diligence.

en.title: Feasibility Analysis and the Go/No-Go Decision
en.short: Testing market, technical, operational, financial and legal feasibility before a go/no-go decision.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text: Feasibility analysis tests whether a proposed venture can work before money and time are committed. It asks whether enough customers will pay, whether the product can be built, whether the team can run it, whether the numbers close, and whether it can be done lawfully. It is not a full business plan. A feasibility study answers yes, no or not yet; a business plan then explains how the venture will be executed, often for lenders or investors.

sections.heading: Five tests
sections.text: Market feasibility estimates demand, target customers, competition and willingness to pay. Technical feasibility asks whether the product or service can be produced with available technology, skills and inputs. Operational feasibility covers daily running: location, suppliers, staffing, quality control and capacity. Financial feasibility compares expected revenues, costs, funding needs and cash flow, often using break-even analysis. Legal feasibility checks registration, licences, permits, taxes, contracts, intellectual property and sector rules. These rules differ by country, so confirm them with the official regulator.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A made-up bakery expects to sell 2,000 loaves a month at ₦500 each. Revenue is ₦1,000,000. Variable cost is ₦300 a loaf, so contribution is ₦200. Fixed costs are ₦300,000 a month. Break-even volume = 300,000 ÷ 200 = 1,500 loaves, or ₦750,000. Forecast margin of safety = (2,000 − 1,500) ÷ 2,000 = 25%. If demand is likely below 1,500 loaves, the financial test fails unless costs or price change.

sections.heading: Decision
sections.text: Set pass criteria before testing: for example, break-even within twelve months, a licence obtainable, and at least a stated number of paying customers. A go decision needs every critical test passed, or a credible plan to fix a weakness. A no-go follows if a fatal flaw cannot be removed. A conditional go means more evidence is needed. Feasibility is quick and evidence-based; the business plan is longer and describes strategy, marketing, operations, team and financial forecasts.

keyPoints: Feasibility analysis tests market, technical, operational, financial and legal viability before major commitment.
A go decision requires all critical tests to pass or a credible fix for any failing test.
Contribution per unit = selling price − variable cost per unit.
Break-even volume = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit.
Margin of safety = (forecast sales volume − break-even volume) ÷ forecast sales volume.
Legal requirements vary by country, and a feasibility study is not a business plan.

en.title: Marketing for New Ventures
en.short: Segmentation, targeting, positioning, the marketing mix, branding, pricing and low-cost promotion.

sections.heading: Segmentation and targeting
sections.text: Segmentation divides a market into groups with similar needs, buying behaviour or ability to pay. A venture with limited cash and people should not serve everyone. It chooses a target segment it can reach and satisfy profitably. Useful tests are whether the segment is measurable, large enough, reachable and distinct. A narrow target is a niche. The venture then writes a short customer profile: who buys, the problem, where they look and what they can afford.

sections.heading: Positioning and mix
sections.text: Positioning is the place a brand holds in a customer’s mind. It should be simple and believable, such as reliable delivery or honest prices. The marketing mix is product, price, place and promotion. Product includes quality and service. Price must cover costs and fit what the target will pay. Place is how the customer gets the offer. Promotion is how the venture communicates. The mix must fit the segment; a premium price with poor service breaks trust.

sections.heading: Branding and pricing
sections.text: Branding is the name, signs and promises that make a venture recognisable. Trust grows when the promise is kept: same quality, clear prices, working contacts and honest claims. Pricing approaches include cost-plus, which adds a margin to cost; value-based pricing, which starts from what the customer believes the offer is worth; penetration pricing, a low launch price to win users; and skimming, a high initial price for early buyers. Cost-plus can ignore demand, and very low prices may signal poor quality. Ensure price covers variable cost, meaning costs that change with each unit sold.

sections.heading: Low-cost promotion
sections.text: Low-cost promotion uses referrals, word of mouth, social media content, local partnerships and free samples. Ada sells school bags in Enugu. She targets parents of primary pupils, positions her bags as strong and fairly priced, and promotes through two parent groups and a repair guarantee. She records referrals and asks happy buyers for testimonials. Her budget is small, so she measures which channel brings customers and drops the rest. Consistent service and visible reviews build trust faster than expensive advertising.

keyPoints: Segment the market, then choose a target you can reach and serve profitably.
Positioning is the simple, believable place you want your brand to hold in the customer’s mind.
The marketing mix is product, price, place and promotion, and all four must fit the target segment.
Cost-plus pricing adds a margin to cost; value-based pricing starts from what customers believe the offer is worth.
Penetration pricing uses a low launch price to win users, while skimming uses a high initial price for early buyers.
Low-cost promotion and consistent service build trust through referrals, testimonials and visible reliability.

en.title: Sales and Customer Development for New Ventures
en.short: The sales process, CRM, retention and simple sales metrics such as conversion rate and CLV.

sections.heading: The sales process
sections.text: Sales in a new venture is a repeatable process, not a single pitch. Prospecting means finding and qualifying people who have a problem your offer solves and can pay. Qualifying saves time: check need, budget, authority and timing. Pitching presents the offer in the customer’s terms: the problem, your solution, evidence and price. Objections are reasons to hesitate, such as price or trust; listen, answer the real concern and confirm agreement. Closing asks for a clear decision, for example a trial, deposit or signed order. Follow-up after the sale checks delivery, solves problems and opens repeat or referral business.

sections.heading: CRM and retention
sections.text: Customer relationship management (CRM) is the system for recording contacts, conversations, promises and purchases so no customer is forgotten. A simple spreadsheet can be a CRM; software helps as volume grows. Retention means keeping customers buying. It usually costs less to sell again to an existing customer than to find a new one, and loyal customers may refer others. Track follow-up dates and complaints, and ask why customers leave.

sections.heading: Metrics and example
sections.text: Two simple metrics guide selling. Conversion rate = customers ÷ qualified prospects × 100. Customer lifetime value (CLV) is the profit expected from one customer over the relationship. A simple form is CLV = average profit per purchase × purchases per year × years retained. Suppose 200 qualified prospects produce 20 customers. Conversion = 20 ÷ 200 × 100 = 10%. If each customer buys twice a year, profit is ₦4,000 per purchase, and they stay three years: CLV = 4,000 × 2 × 3 = ₦24,000. Compare CLV with the cost of gaining a customer.

sections.heading: Learning from customers
sections.text: Customer development means learning from early customers. After each sale, ask what problem they wanted solved, why they chose you and what nearly stopped them. Use the answers to improve the offer, the pitch and the qualification rules. Keep promises small and clear, and review the sales pipeline, the list of prospects by stage, weekly so follow-up does not depend on memory.

keyPoints: Prospecting qualifies prospects by need, budget, authority and timing, and pitching frames the offer around the customer’s problem and evidence.
Objections are handled by listening, answering the real concern and confirming agreement.
Closing asks for a clear decision, and follow-up protects the sale and repeat business.
Conversion rate = customers ÷ qualified prospects × 100.
CLV = average profit per purchase × purchases per year × years retained.
CRM records contacts and follow-up, and retention usually costs less than acquisition.

en.title: Operations and supply for new ventures
en.short: Process design, capacity, quality, inventory, suppliers and location for a new venture.

sections.heading: Process and capacity
sections.text: Process design is the choice of steps, sequence, equipment and people used to make a product or service. A new venture often starts with a job shop, which handles varied small orders, or a batch process, which makes groups of items. Capacity is the most output possible in a period. Utilisation = actual output ÷ capacity. The bottleneck is the step that limits total output. Keep capacity slightly ahead of demand, but do not buy equipment you cannot fill.

sections.heading: Quality and inventory
sections.text: Quality means meeting agreed requirements consistently. Prevention, such as clear standards and simple checks, usually costs less than rework or lost customers. Inventory is stock of inputs or finished goods. Holding inventory ties up cash; running out loses sales. The reorder point is the stock level that triggers a new order: reorder point = (daily demand × lead time) + safety stock. Lead time is the time from ordering to delivery. Safety stock is extra stock kept as a buffer against late deliveries or a jump in demand.

sections.heading: Suppliers and location
sections.text: Supplier selection weighs quality, reliability, price, lead time and payment terms. A second supplier reduces risk but may raise cost. Location affects rent, transport, labour, utilities and closeness to customers or suppliers. For a small venture, a low-cost site far from customers can damage service; a central site can raise rent but shorten delivery.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A juice producer has one filling machine with capacity 2,000 bottles a day. Demand is 1,200 bottles. Utilisation = 1,200 ÷ 2,000 = 60%. Fixed cost is ₦30,000 a day and variable cost is ₦40 a bottle. Price is ₦100, so contribution (price minus variable cost) is ₦60. Break-even = 30,000 ÷ 60 = 500 bottles. Profit at 1,200 bottles = (1,200 × 60) − 30,000 = ₦42,000. If demand reaches 2,500, capacity is short by 500 bottles. The venture can add a shift, buy a second machine or outsource. For inventory, if daily demand is 100 units, lead time is 5 days and safety stock is 200, reorder point = (100 × 5) + 200 = 700 units.

keyPoints: Process design should match demand and avoid overcapacity.
Utilisation = actual output ÷ capacity; the bottleneck limits throughput.
Prevention costs less than rework, so build simple quality checks early.
Reorder point = (daily demand × lead time) + safety stock.
Supplier selection balances quality, reliability, price and lead time.
Location affects cost and customer service, so test the trade-off before signing a lease.

en.title: Financial Management for Entrepreneurs
en.short: Reading statements, forecasting cash, managing working capital and budgeting for a new venture.

sections.heading: Reading the statements
sections.text: Three statements work together. The income statement shows sales, costs and profit over a period. The balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and owner’s equity at a date. The cash flow statement explains cash in and out. Profit is not cash: a sale on credit raises profit before the customer pays. Compare figures with earlier months and ask why they moved.

sections.heading: Cash flow and working capital
sections.text: Cash flow forecasting lists expected receipts and payments by month. Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities: stock (inventory), debtors (customers who owe you) and cash, less creditors (suppliers you owe). A positive figure means short-term resources cover short-term bills. If debtors pay slowly, cash tightens. Example: current assets are ₦800,000 (stock ₦300,000, debtors ₦400,000, cash ₦100,000) and current liabilities are ₦500,000. Working capital is ₦800,000 − ₦500,000 = ₦300,000. If debtors rise by ₦100,000, working capital rises to ₦400,000, but that ₦100,000 is not yet cash.

sections.heading: Budget and control
sections.text: A budget is a plan in money for a future period. A simple cash budget lists opening cash, receipts, payments and closing cash. Financial control means comparing actual results with the budget, finding differences and acting. Keep records, separate business and personal money, and review debtors and stock regularly. Bootstrapping means funding growth from savings and sales rather than outside money; it demands tight control of every payment.

sections.heading: Warning signs
sections.text: Watch for falling cash, rising debtors, stock that does not move, late tax or wage payments, and repeated borrowing to pay daily costs. A cash shortage can appear even when sales grow, because growth uses cash. Forecast weekly when cash is tight. If closing cash turns negative, cut payments, collect debts, delay non-essential spending or arrange finance early. Do not wait for the bank balance to reach zero.

keyPoints: Read the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement together because profit is not cash.
Working capital = current assets − current liabilities.
Closing cash = opening cash + receipts − payments.
Budget variance = actual figure − budgeted figure.
Bootstrapping funds growth from savings and sales and needs tight financial control.
Warning signs include falling cash, rising debtors, slow stock and late payments.

en.title: Sources of Finance for New Ventures
en.short: Main funding sources, matching them to venture stage, and how country rules affect access.

sections.heading: Early money
sections.text: Personal savings are the first and most common source. They cost no interest and do not dilute ownership, but they put the founder’s money at risk. Family and friends may lend or invest, often informally. Write the terms down to avoid disputes. Trade credit means a supplier lets you pay later, 30 to 90 days. It finances stock and is common in wholesale trade, but missed payments can damage reputation and supply.

sections.heading: Debt and grants
sections.text: Bank loans are debt: you repay principal plus interest on a schedule. Banks ask for a business record or collateral, an asset pledged against the loan, so they suit ventures with sales and assets. Microfinance institutions make loans to borrowers without collateral, sometimes using group guarantees. Interest can be high. Grants are non-repayable funds from governments, donors or competitions. They are competitive and tied to purposes. Rules and eligibility differ by country, so check the source.

sections.heading: Equity funding
sections.text: An angel investor is a wealthy individual who invests money, and often advice, in an early venture for equity, which means part ownership. Venture capital (VC) is a professional fund that invests larger amounts in high-growth ventures, after some sales proof, and may take board seats and protective rights. Crowdfunding collects many small contributions through an online platform. Models include reward, donation, debt and equity crowdfunding. Equity crowdfunding is regulated in some countries and restricted in others.

sections.heading: Matching stages
sections.text: Match source to stage. Idea stage: use savings, family money, grants and reward crowdfunding. Early sales: add trade credit and microfinance. For growth, consider bank loans if you have assets and cash flow, or angels and VC if the venture can grow fast. Example: Ngozi in Enugu tests a food-processing idea with savings and a sister’s loan. A supplier gives 30 days trade credit. After six months of sales, a microfinance bank provides working capital. Later, an angel invests. Availability and terms vary by country.

keyPoints: Personal savings and family money are common first funds, but they put the founder’s money and relationships at risk.
Trade credit is short-term supplier finance and must be repaid on time to protect supply.
Bank loans and microfinance are debt, so they require repayment with interest and often collateral.
Grants are non-repayable but competitive and limited to stated purposes.
Angel investors and venture capital provide equity, which means giving up part ownership and accepting dilution, a fall in the founders’ share.
Crowdfunding pools small amounts, and its models and rules vary by country.

en.title: Venture Capital, Valuation and Deal Terms
en.short: How venture capital works, term sheets, pre- and post-money valuation, and dilution with a worked example.

sections.heading: How venture capital works
sections.text: Venture capital (VC) is equity investment by a professional fund in private, high-growth companies. The fund raises money from limited partners (LPs), such as pension funds and wealthy families. It sources deals, screens them, performs due diligence on market, team and finances, negotiates a term sheet, invests, then supports the company and exits later by sale or listing. VC expects many failures and a few large wins, so it targets businesses that can scale. It usually invests in exchange for shares, not repayment.

sections.heading: Term sheet basics
sections.text: A term sheet is a short document setting out proposed deal terms before lawyers draft full contracts. Most clauses are non-binding; confidentiality, exclusivity and costs may bind. Main parts: amount invested, pre-money valuation, share price, investor ownership, liquidation preference (who is paid first on sale), anti-dilution protection (protects the investor if later shares are issued cheaply), board seats, protective provisions (investor vetoes), founder vesting (shares earned over time), drag-along and tag-along rights (rights to force or join a sale), dividends and information rights. Terms allocate risk and control, not just price. Legal rules and standard terms vary by country, so check local company law and securities regulation.

sections.heading: Valuation and dilution
sections.text:
Pre-money valuation is the company’s value before new money. Post-money valuation = pre-money + new investment. Investor ownership = investment ÷ post-money. Dilution is the fall in existing owners’ percentage when new shares are issued.

Example: a start-up has pre-money value US$4,000,000. An investor puts in US$1,000,000.
Post-money = 4,000,000 + 1,000,000 = US$5,000,000.
Investor share = 1,000,000 ÷ 5,000,000 = 20%.
Founders, who owned 100%, now own 80%. If they later raise again, they are diluted further unless they buy more shares in the new round. This is simple dilution; a term sheet may add option pools or preferences that change the arithmetic.

keyPoints: VC is equity investment by a professional fund in high-growth private companies.
Post-money valuation = pre-money valuation + new investment.
Investor ownership = investment ÷ post-money valuation.
Dilution is the fall in existing owners’ percentage after new shares are issued.
A term sheet sets out valuation, ownership, liquidation preference, control and other rights; most clauses are non-binding.
Deal terms and investor rules vary by country, so check local company and securities law.

en.title: Managing the Small Business
en.short: Daily records, staffing, compliance, insurance, suppliers and internal controls for small firms.

sections.heading: From founder to systems
sections.text: As a venture grows, the founder cannot keep every task in their head. The owner-manager, the person who runs the business day to day, needs simple management systems. These are written routines that make work repeatable: who opens the shop, who orders stock, who pays suppliers and how cash is checked. Start with a one-page procedures note and a weekly meeting. The aim is fewer surprises, not bureaucracy.

sections.heading: Records and controls
sections.text: Record keeping means writing down every sale, expense, invoice and payment daily. Keep receipts, number invoices, record stock movements and reconcile the bank account each month. A bank reconciliation compares the bank statement with your cash book and explains the difference. Internal controls are the checks that protect money and stock. Simple controls include one person receiving cash and another recording it, owner approval above a set amount, daily cash counts and locked storage. Segregation of duties means no single person controls a whole transaction from start to finish.

sections.heading: People, suppliers, compliance
sections.text: Staffing needs clear job descriptions, written contracts and a simple payroll. Pay statutory deductions, such as tax and pension amounts withheld from staff wages, where the law requires them; rates and rules differ by country, so check the current official source. Compliance means meeting registration, tax, labour, health and safety and sector rules. Insurance transfers some risks to an insurer: property cover for stock and equipment, public liability for customers, and workers’ compensation where required. For supplier relations, agree price, quality, delivery and credit terms in writing, keep a second supplier for key items, and review performance regularly.

sections.heading: Case: a small bakery
sections.text: Chidi runs a bakery in Enugu with six staff. He keeps a cash book, numbers receipts and counts cash daily. The baker cannot also record sales, so a shop assistant records them. Chidi approves purchases above a set amount and checks the bank reconciliation monthly. He has written contracts, pays tax as required and holds fire insurance on the oven and stock. He buys flour from two suppliers and reviews delivery quality each month.

keyPoints: Simple written routines let the owner-manager delegate without losing control.
Record sales, expenses and payments daily, and reconcile the bank account monthly.
Internal controls separate cash handling from cash recording and require approval for larger payments.
Staff need clear job descriptions, written contracts and correct statutory deductions.
Compliance and insurance duties vary by country; check current official rules and cover key risks.
Agree supplier terms in writing and keep a second source for critical inputs.

en.title: Growth, Scaling and Professionalisation
en.short: Stages of growth, scaling, franchising, licensing, alliances, bottlenecks and formal management.

sections.heading: Stages of growth
sections.text:
Growth is a sequence, not one event. A common model has four stages: start-up, early growth, rapid growth or scaling, and maturity. Start-up proves the offer. Early growth brings rising sales while the founder still does many jobs. Scaling means raising revenue faster than costs by adding capacity, systems and people. Maturity brings slower growth and a need to renew. Stages overlap, and firms can fail or shrink at any point.

Professionalisation is the shift from personal, informal control to formal management: clear roles, written procedures, budgets, reports and delegated decisions. It need not destroy the founder’s energy.

sections.heading: Growth strategies
sections.text: Growth strategies include market penetration (more sales to existing customers), market development (new markets), product development (new offers) and diversification (new products and markets). Firms can also grow through franchising, licensing and alliances. Franchising lets a franchisor grant a franchisee the right to use its brand and system for fees and royalties (payments based on sales), while the franchisee owns the local outlet. Licensing gives another firm rights to use intellectual property, such as a patent or brand, for a fee. A strategic alliance is a cooperation agreement, for example sharing distribution or technology, without full ownership. Each can spread risk and speed up growth but reduces control.

sections.heading: Strains and bottlenecks
sections.text: Growth strains cash, quality and people. A bottleneck is the step that limits total output, such as one overworked manager or a single machine. Hiring must follow role design: define the task, authority and measures before recruiting. The founder must delegate and build a management layer. Informal habits that worked with ten staff can fail with fifty. Formal budgets, stock records, job descriptions and meetings create control, but too much paperwork can slow decisions.

sections.heading: Case: informal to formal
sections.text: Case: Amina’s food firm in Kano, Nigeria, saw orders double. She was the bottleneck, approving every purchase. She appointed an operations supervisor, wrote purchase and quality procedures, and licensed her spice blend to a distributor for a royalty.

keyPoints: Growth usually moves through start-up, early growth, scaling and maturity, and stages overlap.
Scaling raises revenue faster than costs by adding capacity, systems and people.
Franchising, licensing and alliances spread risk and speed growth but reduce control.
A bottleneck is the step that limits total output, so fix it before adding more sales.
Professionalisation means clear roles, written procedures, budgets and delegated decisions.
Hire against defined roles and build management systems before informal habits fail.

en.title: Digital Entrepreneurship and E-commerce
en.short: E-commerce, marketplaces, platforms, digital marketing, analytics, payments and online security.

sections.heading: Ways to sell online
sections.text:
E-commerce means buying and selling goods or services over the internet. A venture can run its own online store, which gives control over branding and customer data, or sell through an online marketplace such as Jumia or Konga, where many sellers share one site. A marketplace brings traffic and trust but takes fees and limits customer contact.

A platform is a system that connects two or more groups and creates value from their interactions; network effects mean it becomes more useful as more users join. A made-up Lagos homeware seller, AdaHome, might use its own site for repeat customers and a marketplace for discovery.

sections.heading: Marketing and analytics
sections.text:
Digital marketing uses online channels such as search, social media, email and content to attract customers. Analytics turns visitor data into decisions. The funnel runs from impressions (times an ad is seen) to clicks to orders.

Conversion rate = orders ÷ visits.
Customer acquisition cost (CAC) = marketing spend ÷ new customers.

Suppose a store gets 4,000 visits in a month, converts 2.5% and has an average order value of ₦6,000.
Orders = 4,000 × 0.025 = 100.
Revenue = 100 × ₦6,000 = ₦600,000.
If ad spend is ₦150,000 and all 100 orders are first orders from new customers, CAC = ₦150,000 ÷ 100 = ₦1,500 per customer.
Compare CAC with the gross profit a customer brings, not revenue alone.

sections.heading: Payments and security
sections.text:
Online payments usually run through a payment gateway, a service that authorises cards, bank transfers or mobile money and helps settle funds to the merchant. Rules on licensing, fees, chargebacks (reversed card payments) and know-your-customer checks vary by country, so check the central bank and gateway terms.

Cybersecurity duties include using HTTPS, strong passwords, two-factor authentication, updated software and staff training against phishing. If you handle card data, the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) sets security requirements. Privacy laws vary: the EU GDPR, Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 and South Africa’s POPIA set duties. Collect only the data you need, secure it, and tell users what you do with it.

keyPoints: E-commerce is selling online; a marketplace hosts many sellers, while a platform connects groups and gains from network effects.
Conversion rate = orders ÷ visits, and customer acquisition cost = marketing spend ÷ new customers.
Compare customer acquisition cost with the gross profit a customer brings, not with revenue.
A payment gateway authorises and settles online payments; licensing, fees and chargeback rules vary by country.
Basic security includes HTTPS, strong passwords, two-factor authentication, updates and training against phishing.
Data privacy laws vary by country; collect only necessary data, secure it and explain its use.

en.title: Social Entrepreneurship and Social Enterprise
en.short: Models, impact, hybrid finance and the tension between mission and trading income.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text:
Social entrepreneurship means spotting and pursuing opportunities to create social value, often by running an enterprise. A social enterprise is an organisation that trades in goods or services to pursue a social mission and usually reinvests most surplus in that mission. It sits between a charity, which relies mainly on donations, and a conventional business, which distributes profit to owners.

Common models include the embedded model, where the mission is in the product itself, such as fair trade; the integrated model, where the mission is in how the organisation works, such as employing people who face barriers to work; and the external model, where a business funds a separate social programme. Cooperatives and work integration social enterprises are also common.

sections.heading: Models and income
sections.text: Trading income can come from selling to the public, to government or to firms. Cross-subsidy is common: one group pays a commercial price so another pays less. Hybrid financing blends earned income with grants, donations, debt and equity. Blended finance combines public or philanthropic money with private capital. Legal forms differ by country: the UK has the community interest company (CIC), and some US states have the benefit corporation. Certification schemes such as B Corp are separate from legal forms. Check local rules before choosing a form.

sections.heading: Impact and tension
sections.text:
Impact is the lasting change a venture creates. A theory of change links inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes. Social return on investment (SROI) tries to put a money value on social outcomes, but it depends on assumptions, so use it carefully.

The main tension is mission drift: pressure to earn income can pull a venture away from its social purpose. A made-up training enterprise charges firms ₦80,000 per course and low-income trainees ₦20,000. It runs 10 firm courses and 20 trainee courses: revenue is ₦800,000 + ₦400,000 = ₦1,200,000. If each of the 30 courses costs ₦50,000, total cost is ₦1,500,000, a loss of ₦300,000. It must raise prices, cut costs, win a grant or serve fewer trainees.

keyPoints: Social entrepreneurship pursues social value, while a social enterprise trades to fund a social mission.
Embedded, integrated and external models describe how the mission links to trading.
Hybrid financing combines earned income with grants, donations, debt and equity.
Cross-subsidy uses surplus from one customer group to serve another.
Impact measurement links activities to outcomes, and SROI depends on assumptions.
Mission drift is the risk that commercial income weakens social purpose.

en.title: Family Business: Governance and Succession
en.short: Family and business systems, governance, conflict, professionalisation and planning leadership transfer.

sections.heading: Two systems
sections.text: A family business is owned or controlled by a family. It contains two systems. The family system rewards loyalty, seniority, harmony and support. The business system rewards competence, performance, efficiency and accountability. The same people can be parent and boss, or sibling and shareholder. A common three-circle model separates family, ownership and management, so a person may belong to one, two or all three. Governance is the rules, roles and forums for decisions and accountability. Without it, family feelings and business needs become confused.

sections.heading: Governance and conflict
sections.text: Typical problems include unclear roles, nepotism (giving jobs or favours to relatives regardless of merit), unequal pay, sibling rivalry and a founder who keeps all authority. Conflict often comes from expectations never written down. A family constitution is a written statement of agreed principles on employment, pay, entry and exit, and disputes. A family council gives members a forum to discuss family issues outside business meetings. A board, including an independent director, reviews strategy and performance.

sections.heading: Professionalisation and succession
sections.text: Professionalisation means replacing informal arrangements with formal systems: job descriptions, budgets, performance appraisal, written procedures and qualified managers. It improves decisions and controls, but can clash with family values. Introduce it gradually and make employment depend on competence. Succession is the transfer of leadership and ownership to the next generation. Problems include founder reluctance, no chosen successor, fairness among children, unprepared heirs and unclear ownership. Plan early: agree a date, choose on competence, train the successor, communicate decisions and take legal and tax advice. In a made-up case, Ngozi Okeke founded a printing firm in Enugu, Nigeria. Her son managed production and her daughter sales, but roles and pay were unwritten. After her stroke, the siblings argued over expansion. An adviser helped them write a family constitution, appoint an independent director and set a five-year plan. The daughter became chief executive after training, the son kept operations, and a lawyer prepared the share transfer.

keyPoints: A family business combines a family system based on loyalty with a business system based on performance.
Governance uses rules, roles and forums such as a family council, board and family constitution to separate family, ownership and management decisions.
Conflict commonly arises from unclear roles, nepotism, unequal pay, sibling rivalry and a founder who keeps authority.
Professionalisation means formal systems and qualified managers, introduced gradually so that competence guides employment.
Succession planning covers both leadership and ownership and should begin early with training, written plans and open communication.
Choose successors on competence and willingness, and take independent legal and tax advice for the transfer.

en.title: Intrapreneurship and Corporate Venturing
en.short: How established firms encourage internal entrepreneurs, and why corporate ventures fail.

sections.heading: Two related ideas
sections.text: Intrapreneurship means employees acting like entrepreneurs inside an existing organisation. They spot an opportunity, assemble resources and take measured risks without leaving their employer. Corporate venturing is the firm’s formal effort to create or back new businesses. It can use internal ventures (new businesses owned inside the firm), corporate incubators (in-house support programmes), accelerators (short, intensive programmes), joint ventures or minority investments in outside start-ups. An innovation unit is a team set aside to develop ideas away from daily operations; a skunkworks is a small team kept away from normal bureaucracy and given freedom to move fast.

sections.heading: How firms encourage it
sections.text: Firms encourage intrapreneurship in four ways. They give people slack: time and small budgets to test ideas. They create stage gates: a venture earns more money only after passing evidence checks. They reward effort with bonuses, recognition, promotion or phantom equity, which pays like shares without ownership. They build a culture of psychological safety, where people can report failure without blame, plus senior sponsors who protect the venture.

sections.heading: Not a start-up
sections.text: An intrapreneur has advantages: existing customers, brand, suppliers, cash and legal support. An independent start-up must build these. But the intrapreneur faces approval layers, corporate accounting, brand rules and pay caps. A start-up can offer equity and quick decisions; a corporate venture often cannot. This is why the same idea may move faster outside.

sections.heading: Why ventures fail
sections.text: Common reasons include no clear link to strategy, no senior sponsor, and funding withdrawn too early. Wrong metrics kill ventures: demanding full profit in year one punishes learning. Isolation from the core business can starve a venture of customers, while too much control can smother it. Reward systems that pay salaried staff, not founders, lose the best people. A made-up case: Nairobi Foods starts an internal venture for solar milk coolers. It gives a small team a budget, a senior sponsor and milestone reviews. Early sales are slow. The firm studies feedback, changes the price and keeps funding. The venture survives because the firm judged learning, not only early profit.

keyPoints: Intrapreneurship is entrepreneurial behaviour by employees inside an existing firm.
Corporate venturing creates or backs new businesses through internal ventures, incubators, joint ventures or external investments.
Stage gates release more funding only when a venture shows evidence.
Rewards must match risk-taking, for example bonuses, recognition or phantom equity.
Corporate ventures often fail through weak strategy links, poor sponsorship, wrong metrics or early funding cuts.
Intrapreneurs gain corporate resources but lose the speed and equity upside of independent start-ups.

en.title: Entrepreneurial Ethics and Social Responsibility
en.short: Ethical issues entrepreneurs face, CSR, sustainability and how stakeholder trust pays.

sections.heading: Honesty in the market
sections.text: Ethics is the study of right and wrong conduct. Business ethics applies it where law does not settle the question: the legal minimum is not always the ethical standard. Honesty in marketing means claims about a product are true and not misleading. Fake testimonials, hidden charges and false health claims are unethical and, in most countries, illegal. Consumer protection law differs by country; Nigeria’s Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018 is one example.

sections.heading: Fair treatment of workers
sections.text: Fair treatment of workers covers wages paid on time, safe conditions, written terms, rest days, and no forced or child labour. Much of this is legal duty under national labour law, but enforcement is uneven and the ethical duty does not depend on inspection. Fairness also means hearing complaints and not punishing a worker who reports a safety risk. Fair employers keep trained staff and face fewer disputes.

sections.heading: Conflicts and compliance
sections.text: A conflict of interest arises when a personal interest could sway a business decision, for example a manager who owns the firm’s main supplier. The usual remedy is to disclose it and let someone else decide. Legal compliance means keeping to tax, licensing, environmental and employment rules; shortcuts bring fines, closure and lost reputation. Bribery is illegal under laws such as the UK Bribery Act 2010, and small facilitation payments, meaning small payments to speed up routine services, are no safe exception.

sections.heading: Responsibility and trust
sections.text:
Corporate social responsibility (CSR) is a firm’s voluntary commitment to act for society’s good beyond legal duty. Sustainability means meeting present needs without harming future generations’ ability to meet theirs, summed up as the triple bottom line: profit, people, planet. Stakeholders are those affected by the firm: customers, workers, suppliers, lenders, the community. Trust lowers the cost of dealing.

Adaeze sells sachet water in Enugu, Nigeria. A supplier offers cheaper caps that leak slightly. She keeps the dearer caps and prints the batch date on every bag. When a rival’s bags leaked, retailers moved to her within weeks.

keyPoints: The legal minimum is not the ethical standard; ethics asks what is fair, not only what is allowed.
Marketing claims must be true and not misleading, and consumer protection law differs by country.
Fair pay, safe work and written terms are legal duties in most countries and ethical duties everywhere.
Disclose a conflict of interest and step back from the decision it affects.
CSR is voluntary action beyond legal duty; sustainability also weighs the needs of future generations.
Ethical conduct builds stakeholder trust, which lowers the cost of doing business.

en.title: Risk, Failure and Resilience
en.short: How ventures identify and manage risk, learn from failure and handle insolvency.

sections.heading: Identifying and assessing risk
sections.text: Risk is the chance that an event harms the venture. Uncertainty means outcomes cannot be listed or probabilities estimated. Entrepreneurs list risks by area: market, operations, finance, people, legal and reputation. A risk register records each risk, its cause and its owner. A risk matrix scores likelihood and impact from 1 to 5. Score = likelihood × impact. A power outage scored 4 × 5 = 20 is high priority; a stationery delay scored 1 × 2 = 2 is low. Scores guide attention, not certainty.

sections.heading: Mitigating risk
sections.text: Mitigation reduces risk to an acceptable level. Common responses are avoid (stop the activity), reduce (train staff, hold safety stock), transfer (insurance, contracts) and accept (keep a reserve). Insurance transfers defined losses, such as fire or theft, to an insurer for a premium. It does not cover every loss, so read exclusions. Crisis planning prepares for emergencies: name a leader, keep contact lists, back up data, arrange alternative suppliers and practise a response. Business continuity planning aims to keep essential operations running.

sections.heading: Failure and learning
sections.text: Ventures fail for many reasons: no demand, running out of cash, weak margins, poor records, founder disputes, competition and external shocks. Failure is not proof that the founder is worthless. A post-mortem is a structured review after a setback. It asks what happened, why, what was learned and what will change. Record and share the lessons. Resilience means adapting and recovering, not pretending risk has gone.

sections.heading: Insolvency and resilience
sections.text: Insolvency means being unable to pay debts as they fall due. Liquidation winds up a company and sells assets; administration may try to rescue it, while receivership usually means a creditor takes control of assets to recover what is owed. Bankruptcy usually refers to an individual, though terms differ. Legal procedures vary by country, so check local law and take advice early. Example: Ngozi runs a bakery in Enugu. She scores flour price rises and power cuts as high risks, buys fire insurance, keeps a cash reserve and trains a second baker. When a key worker leaves, production continues. She reviews near misses.

keyPoints: Risk is the chance of harm; uncertainty means outcomes or probabilities are unknown.
A risk register and a likelihood × impact matrix help set priorities.
Mitigation options are avoid, reduce, transfer and accept; insurance transfers defined losses.
Crisis and business continuity plans keep essential operations running during shocks.
Ventures often fail from weak demand, cash shortage or founder disputes, so learn through a post-mortem.
Insolvency means inability to pay debts as they fall due, and legal procedures vary by country.

en.title: Exit Strategies and Harvesting Value
en.short: Trade sale, management buyout, IPO and succession, plus sale readiness, exit valuation and local rules.

sections.heading: Routes to exit
sections.text: An exit strategy is a plan for owners to sell or transfer their stake. This is sometimes called harvesting value. Main routes are a trade sale, a sale to an outside buyer such as a competitor; a management buyout (MBO), where existing managers buy the business; an initial public offering (IPO), where shares are sold to the public on a stock exchange; and succession, where ownership passes to family, employees or a new owner over time. Each suits different owners.

sections.heading: Preparing for sale
sections.text: Buyers pay for a business they can check. Preparation often takes one to three years. The owner should clean up accounts, separate personal and business expenses, secure key contracts, reduce dependence on one customer or the founder, and build a management team that can run the firm without them. Due diligence follows: the buyer inspects records, tax, legal claims and staff. An organised document set, called a data room, helps. Weak records lower the price or kill the deal.

sections.heading: Valuation at exit
sections.text:
Exit valuation uses maintainable earnings, the profit the business can keep earning under a new owner. A common method is a multiple of maintainable profit. The multiple rises with growth, recurring revenue and low risk, and falls with customer concentration. Enterprise value is the value of the operating business. Equity value is what shareholders own: equity value = enterprise value − net debt, where net debt is debt minus cash.

Example: maintainable profit is ₦12,000,000. Similar firms sell at 5 times profit. Enterprise value = 12,000,000 × 5 = ₦60,000,000. Net debt is ₦10,000,000. Equity value = 60,000,000 − 10,000,000 = ₦50,000,000. A founder with 70% receives 0.70 × 50,000,000 = ₦35,000,000 before tax and costs.

sections.heading: Rules vary by country
sections.text: IPO listing rules differ by country and exchange. They usually cover minimum trading history, audited accounts, a prospectus, free float (the shares the public can trade) and ongoing disclosure. Tax on an exit also differs: capital gains tax, reliefs for small business owners and treatment of share sales vary. Check the current rules of the relevant exchange and tax authority, and take professional advice before signing.

keyPoints: An exit strategy converts ownership into cash or another benefit through a trade sale, MBO, IPO or succession.
Preparation for sale means clean records, secure contracts, reduced founder dependence and a data room.
Exit value often uses a multiple of maintainable profit.
Equity value = enterprise value − net debt.
Exit proceeds = ownership share × equity value, before tax and costs.
Listing rules and tax treatment vary by country, so check current official sources.

en.title: Advanced Theories of Entrepreneurship: Opportunity, Action and Context
en.short: Opportunity theory, causation and effectuation, bricolage, resource-based and institutional views compared.

sections.heading: Opportunity and action
sections.text: Opportunity theory asks where venture ideas come from and why some people act on them. The individual-opportunity nexus (Shane and Venkataraman) links an external opportunity to an entrepreneur’s knowledge and alertness. Kirzner stressed alertness to missed market chances; Schumpeter stressed innovation that disrupts existing arrangements. Some scholars treat opportunities as discovered, others as created through action. The lens explains selection, not the full process of building a firm.

sections.heading: Causation and effectuation
sections.text: Causation is goal-driven: choose a goal, predict the future, gather resources and execute a plan. Effectuation (Sarasvathy) is means-driven: start with who you are, what you know and whom you know; set an affordable loss rather than an expected return; form partnerships; and turn surprises into new possibilities. It suits high uncertainty. Causation fits predictable markets; effectuation fits new markets where prediction is weak.

sections.heading: Resources and institutions
sections.text: The resource-based view (Barney) explains performance differences through resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and hard to substitute. Dynamic capabilities extend this to how firms adapt. Bricolage (Baker and Nelson) describes making do by recombining resources at hand under scarcity. Institutional views (North; Scott) show that formal rules and informal norms shape costs, legitimacy and access. In emerging markets, gaps in market-supporting institutions, called institutional voids, raise reliance on personal networks and bricolage.

sections.heading: Comparing lenses
sections.text: These lenses answer different questions. Opportunity theory explains idea selection; causation and effectuation explain decision logic; bricolage explains resource use; the resource-based view explains advantage; institutional theory explains context. In a made-up case, Ngozi in Enugu sees demand for packaged spices (opportunity), starts with family recipes and a rented kitchen (effectuation and bricolage), and builds trusted supplier ties where formal contracts are weak (institutional view). No single lens is complete; use them together.
