keyPoints: Opportunity theory links external chances to entrepreneurial knowledge and alertness.
Causation selects means to reach a chosen goal; effectuation starts from available means and affordable loss.
Effectuation is more useful when uncertainty makes prediction unreliable.
Bricolage is making do by recombining resources at hand.
The resource-based view explains advantage through valuable, rare, hard-to-imitate resources.
Institutional views show how formal rules and informal norms, including institutional voids, shape entrepreneurial action.

en.title: Research Methods for Entrepreneurship
en.short: Designing an entrepreneurship dissertation: questions, designs, sampling, validity, ethics and analysis.

sections.heading: Framing the study
sections.text: Start with a problem that matters and is researchable. A dissertation problem is a gap between what is known and what practice or theory needs. Turn it into one or two questions naming the population, concepts and setting. For example, Amina studies why food vendors in Kano adopt mobile payments. 'Why do vendors adopt technology?' is too broad. 'Which factors explain mobile payment adoption among food vendors in Kano?' is narrower. The literature review is not a list of summaries. It should show the debate, define constructs, and end with the gap your question addresses.

sections.heading: Designs and sampling
sections.text: Choose a design that fits the question. Quantitative designs test relationships with numbers, often using surveys or experiments. Qualitative designs explore meaning and process through interviews, observation or documents. Mixed methods combine both, for example a survey followed by interviews to explain the numbers. Define the population, then sample. Probability sampling, such as simple random sampling, supports generalisation. Non-probability sampling, such as purposive or convenience sampling, is common in qualitative work but limits generalisation. Report how you selected participants.

sections.heading: Measurement and quality
sections.text: Measurement turns concepts into observable items. Operationalise each construct, for example define 'adoption' as reported use in the last three months. Use validated scales where they exist, and pilot your instrument. Validity means the instrument measures what it claims. Internal validity concerns causal claims; external validity concerns generalisation. Reliability means consistency: a scale or coding scheme gives similar results on repeated use. In qualitative work, keep an audit trail, a written record of your decisions, triangulate by comparing different sources of evidence, and check interpretations with participants.

sections.heading: Analysis, ethics, pitfalls
sections.text: Match analysis to design. Quantitative work uses descriptive statistics, then tests such as regression when assumptions hold. Qualitative work uses coding and thematic analysis, moving from codes to themes. Ethics require informed consent, voluntary participation, confidentiality, secure data, and approval from your institution’s ethics committee. Pitfalls include a vague question, literature used as a list, convenience samples treated as representative, leading questions, ignoring negative cases, and claiming causation from correlation.

keyPoints: A dissertation question should name the population, concepts and setting, and flow from a clear gap.
Quantitative designs test relationships; qualitative designs explore meaning; mixed methods combine both.
Probability sampling supports generalisation, while non-probability sampling limits it.
Validity is about measuring the right thing; reliability is about consistency.
Ethics require informed consent, confidentiality and, usually, committee approval.
Match analysis to design, and do not claim causation from correlation.

en.title: Entrepreneurial Ecosystems and Policy
en.short: The actors, institutions, measurement and policy that shape new ventures in a region.

sections.heading: Actors and institutions
sections.text: An entrepreneurial ecosystem is the set of interconnected actors, institutions and conditions that help or hinder new ventures in a place. Actors include entrepreneurs, finance providers such as angels, venture capital, banks and microfinance, universities, incubators and accelerators, large firms, professional services and government agencies. Incubators offer space and advice; accelerators add short, intensive programmes and often seed money. Clusters are geographic concentrations of related firms and suppliers. Culture means shared attitudes to risk, failure and collaboration. A culture that accepts failure lowers the cost of trying again.

sections.heading: Measuring ecosystems
sections.text: Measurement uses surveys and indices. The Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) surveys adults about attitudes, early-stage activity and aspirations across countries. Startup Genome ranks cities by funding, talent and market reach. No single score captures an ecosystem; use several and check the year and country coverage. Measurement matters because policy targets what is measured.

sections.heading: Policy that helps or hinders
sections.text: Policy can support ventures by simplifying registration, enforcing contracts, allowing easy bankruptcy, funding early research, using public procurement and offering tax incentives. It can hinder through red tape, corruption, weak property rights, high compliance costs and capital controls. Country differences are large. Mobile money in Kenya changed how ventures collect payments; unreliable electricity raises costs in parts of Nigeria; South Africa has deep financial markets but concentrated venture capital. Policy must fit local institutions, not copy Silicon Valley.

sections.heading: Illustrative case
sections.text: Consider a made-up case in Kano, Nigeria. Amina wants to launch a cold-chain service. A university lab tests her prototype; an incubator offers desk space; a government grant covers part of the cost; a bank refuses a loan without collateral. Policy that allows movable assets as collateral and funds university labs would help. A culture that stigmatises failure would discourage her second attempt.

keyPoints: An ecosystem includes finance, universities, incubators, government, clusters and culture.
Incubators support early ventures; accelerators add intensive programmes and often seed money.
GEM and Startup Genome are two ways to measure ecosystems, but no single score is enough.
Policy can lower the costs and risks of starting and running a venture through simpler registration, contract enforcement and bankruptcy law.
Red tape, corruption and weak property rights hinder new ventures.
Country conditions differ, so policy should fit local institutions.

en.title: Technology Entrepreneurship and Innovation Systems
en.short: Deep tech, intellectual property, spin-outs, commercialisation, innovation systems and scaling science ventures.

sections.heading: Deep technology and IP
sections.text: Deep technology ventures rest on scientific or engineering advances, not mainly on a new app or business model. Examples include new materials, biotech, robotics and clean energy. They often need long research and development, specialised equipment and patient capital. Intellectual property (IP) is the legal protection of creations such as inventions, designs, software, brands and secret know-how. Patents protect new, inventive and industrially useful inventions for a limited term, but only in the countries where they are granted. Copyright, trademarks and trade secrets cover other assets. IP law differs by country, so a founder must check national rules and filing costs.

sections.heading: From lab to spin-out
sections.text: Research commercialisation moves a discovery from the laboratory to users. A university technology transfer office (TTO) receives an invention disclosure, assesses novelty and market need, and decides whether to patent, license or help form a spin-out. A spin-out is a new company created to exploit research, often with the university holding equity or a licence. Spin-out policies, equity splits and royalty terms vary by university and country. In a made-up case, Dr Amina at a Nigerian university invents a low-cost water-quality sensor. She discloses it to the TTO. The university files a patent application and licenses the technology to a new company, with the university taking equity and a royalty. The team runs a pilot with a water utility. The terms must be negotiated under the university’s policy.

sections.heading: Innovation systems and scaling
sections.text: An innovation system is the network of universities, firms, government agencies, investors and intermediaries that together turn knowledge into products. Policy affects this system through research funding, tax incentives, procurement and IP rules. Scaling a science-based venture is rarely just a marketing task. The firm may need pilot plants, regulatory approval, quality certification, manufacturing partners and long sales cycles. It must also manage IP in each target market and raise capital for each stage. Founders should build partnerships early and check the rules of every country where they plan to operate.

keyPoints: Deep technology ventures are built on scientific or engineering advances and need long research, specialised facilities and patient capital.
Intellectual property is territorial: patents must be applied for and granted under the law of each country.
A university spin-out is a company formed to commercialise research, often under a licence or with university equity.
Research commercialisation usually begins with an invention disclosure to a technology transfer office.
An innovation system links universities, firms, government, investors and intermediaries that turn knowledge into products.
Scaling a science-based venture requires regulatory, manufacturing, IP and financing plans for each target market.
